title: Radical bromination: Br2 picks the 3° C–H
why: Light splits Br2 into Br atoms, and Br• removes the H that gives the most stable radical, 3° > 2° > 1°. H abstraction by Br• is uphill, so its transition state looks like the radical and the 3° site wins almost exclusively: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

traps.explains: That's bromination at the 2° CH2. A 2° radical is less stable than the 3° one, and Br• is very selective, so the 3° product dominates.
There are more 1° hydrogens, but counting H atoms only matters for the unselective Cl•. Br• goes for the weakest C–H, the 3° one.
A 1° radical is the least stable. Radical halogenation doesn't favour the end of the chain; with Br2 it favours the most substituted carbon.

distractors.explains: Alkanes have no π bond or leaving group; HBr does nothing to them.
Peroxides make HBr add anti-Markovnikov, giving 1-bromo-2-methylbutane, not the 3° bromide.

title: Radical bromination of methylcyclohexane
why: Br• is highly selective and removes the hydrogen that leaves the most stable radical. The ring carbon bearing the methyl group is 3°, so bromine ends up there: 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.

traps.explains: That's a 2° position. The 3° radical is more stable, and Br• is selective enough to almost always pick it.
The CH3 gives a 1° radical, the least stable. Br• avoids it.
There are many 2° ring hydrogens, but Br• doesn't go by numbers; it goes by radical stability, so the single 3° H wins.

title: Radical chlorination: one kind of H, one product
why: Light splits Cl2 into Cl atoms, Cl• removes an H to give a cyclohexyl radical, and that radical takes Cl from Cl2, passing the chain on. Cl• is not very selective, but here every H is equivalent, so there is only one monochlorination product: chlorocyclohexane (excess cyclohexane keeps it from going further).

traps.explains: Adding Cl2 across a ring needs a C=C. Cyclohexane has no π bond, so Cl replaces one H (substitution) instead.
Further chlorination can happen, but using excess alkane keeps the main product monochlorinated.
Radical halogenation substitutes; it doesn't eliminate. No base is present to make an alkene.

title: NBS: allylic bromination, not addition
why: The allylic C–H is weak because the allylic radical it gives is resonance-stabilized, so Br• removes it. NBS releases Br2 only slowly (from the HBr formed), keeping [Br2] so low that addition to the C=C can't compete with the radical chain: 3-bromocyclohexene (racemic).

traps.explains: That's addition of Br2 across the C=C, which needs a high Br2 concentration. NBS keeps Br2 scarce, so allylic substitution wins.
C4 is not allylic (it's one carbon further away), so its radical gets no resonance help. Br goes on the carbon next to the C=C.
A vinylic C–H is strong and its radical isn't resonance-stabilized; Br• takes the weak allylic H instead.

distractors.explains: At normal concentration Br2 adds across the C=C, giving trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
HBr adds across the C=C, giving bromocyclohexane; the double bond is lost.
